mainEntity.name: Our therapists wipe the tables and mats between patients. Is that enough?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wiping is cleaning, and cleaning is not disinfection. They are two steps. Treatment tables, mats, weights, and bands that contact intact skin are non-critical items that need to be cleaned and then disinfected between patients at the level the degree of soiling requires, per the CDC Infection Prevention Checklist non-critical item definition and CDC Core Practices 5f. Between-patient turnover stays with your clinicians, because they are the ones in the room. What we own is the end-of-day terminal pass across every table, mat, and plinth, plus floors, restrooms, and shared areas.

mainEntity.name: How should we handle foam rollers, therabands, and fabric straps? They cannot really be disinfected.

acceptedAnswer.text: That is exactly the issue, and it has a stated answer. Where a manufacturer provides no cleaning and disinfection instructions, CDC's position under Section II item A of the Infection Prevention Checklist and Core Practices 5f is that the item is not suitable for multi-patient use. Porous foam, fabric straps, and cut bands frequently fall there. The practical fixes are single-patient assignment, launderable covers, or replacement with a non-porous equivalent. We inventory the gym, mark which items have usable instructions and which do not, and hand the list to you.

mainEntity.name: Skin-to-equipment contact all day is our real exposure. What do you actually do about it?

acceptedAnswer.text: We treat the gym as a contact-transfer environment rather than an office. Every surface a patient's bare skin meets, including plinth vinyl, mat surfaces, exercise ball skins, bench pads, and the floor of the mat area, is cleaned and then disinfected on a defined interval with an EPA-registered product chosen for that surface. The mat floor gets a wet process rather than a dry mop that redistributes skin debris. Written policies naming the gym, the treatment tables, and the shared equipment are precisely what Section I item A of the CDC Infection Prevention Checklist asks a clinic to hold.

Our Concord program for rehabilitation clinics is written around one risk — direct skin contact with shared equipment all day, with no barrier — MRSA and fungal transfer — and one set of surfaces: treatment tables, mats, therabands, free weights, exercise balls, parallel bars, treadmills.

How we clean rehabilitation clinics in Concord

Where contamination concentrates

  • Free weights, dumbbells and kettlebells
  • Resistance bands and handles
  • Treadmill and bike handles and consoles
  • Parallel bars and balance equipment
  • Therapy balls and foam rollers
  • Check-in counter

Our sequence, step by step

  1. Agree which equipment staff wipe between patients and which the cleaning crew handles at end of day.
  2. Clean and disinfect treatment tables and mats with products compatible with vinyl and upholstery.
  3. Wipe down weights, bars and cardio equipment handles and consoles.
  4. Keep gym cloths separate from restroom cloths.
  5. Damp-mop gym floors and vacuum carpeted areas.

A starting schedule

  • Gym floor: daily.
  • Restrooms and changing areas: daily or more often.
  • Waiting room: daily.

Clinics with early-morning patients may prefer a pre-opening clean.

Documentation you receive

  • Gym and treatment-room checklist
  • Product list with EPA registration numbers and contact times
  • Safety Data Sheets
  • Signed service logs

Survey findings we help Concord facilities prevent

Real, published regulatory findings — every citation links to its source.

CDC Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices 5b; CDC Infection Prevention Checklist, Section II item A

High-touch surfaces close to the patient — plinth rails, parallel bars, equipment grips — not cleaned and disinfected on a more frequent schedule than other surfaces.

CDC Infection Prevention Checklist for Outpatient Settings, Section II item B; CDC Core Practices 5b

Disinfectant wipes used with insufficient contact time — the surface dries before the label kill time, or the product is past shelf life or badly stored.

CDC Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices 5f

Clean and soiled equipment stored together, with no physical separation to prevent cross-contamination.
